title: Creative strategy
summary: Creative is the biggest lever a buyer controls: it decides who stops, who clicks and, on broad audiences, who Meta finds next. This module covers hooks, angles, formats, testing, fatigue, localisation, honest copy and using AI tools responsibly, with numbers you can apply to your own ads. It ends with producing ads cheaply on a phone, so you can test enough concepts to find winners.

lessons.title: Hooks and the first 3 seconds
objectives: By the end you can name six honest hook types and write one of each.
You can measure hook rate and hold rate from Ads Manager columns.
You can show with numbers how a better hook lowers cost per click.
You can set up hook rate and hold rate columns and use them to pick the next iteration.

steps.h: Nothing else matters if they scroll past
steps.p: People scroll fast. In the first one to three seconds they decide whether your ad is worth their attention. A strong body with a weak opening is never seen. The hook is the opening that earns the rest of the ad.

d.s: Then the next, then the click

steps.say: Let's start with a hard truth. People scroll fast, and in the first one to three seconds they decide whether your ad deserves their attention. You could have a brilliant body, but if the opening is weak, nobody ever sees it. That opening is the hook. As the screen says, its job is to earn the next second, then the next, and then the click.

steps.p: Every hook below can be written honestly. Pick the type that fits your angle and audience, then test several types against the same body so you learn which opening works.
d: Question|Do you know what a spread is?
Callout|Nairobi, new to trading? Watch this.
Demonstration|show the app working in second one
Bold true statement|Most beginners skip the demo account.
Pattern interrupt|an unexpected but relevant visual
Story opener|Last year I lost my first deposit in a week.
steps.say: Here are six hook types, and every one can be written honestly. A question, like do you know what a spread is. A callout, naming the viewer, like Nairobi, new to trading. A demonstration, showing the app working in second one. A bold true statement. A pattern interrupt, an unexpected but relevant visual. And a story opener. Pick the type that fits your angle and audience, then test several types against the same body, so you learn which opening actually works.

steps.h: What happens in the first 3 seconds
steps.p: A good opening stacks several signals at once, because many people watch with sound off and some only glance. Each layer tells the viewer the same thing: this is for you.
steps.say: Look at this flow. A good opening stacks several signals at once. It starts with a striking first frame at zero seconds, then on-screen text, then a spoken line, then a reason to keep watching. Why stack them? Because many people watch with the sound off, and some only glance. Every layer tells the viewer the same thing: this is for you.

steps.p: You cannot judge a hook by feel. Build custom columns in Ads Manager from the video metrics. Exact column names change, so check the current Ads Manager for 3-second plays and ThruPlays.
steps.say: You can't judge a hook by feel, so you measure it. Look at the table. Hook rate is three-second plays divided by impressions, and it tells you whether the opening stopped people. Hold rate is ThruPlays divided by three-second plays, did the body keep them. Link C T R, click-through rate, is link clicks divided by impressions, did they act. And cost per result tells you whether it made money. Column names change, so check the current Ads Manager for three-second plays and ThruPlays.

steps.title: Open column settings

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.text: Name it Hook rate and divide 3-second video plays by impressions. Format it as a percentage.

steps.say: Let's build a hook rate column. Tap Next to follow each step. First, open the columns menu, choose to customise columns, and create a custom metric. Second, name it Hook rate, and set the formula to three-second video plays divided by impressions, formatted as a percentage. Third, create Hold rate the same way, ThruPlays divided by three-second plays, and save both in a preset. steps.p: Example: an ad got 10,000 impressions and 3,000 people watched at least three seconds. The hook rate is 30%. Track it for every video so you can compare openings fairly.
steps.say: Here's hook rate in one line. In this example, an ad got ten thousand impressions, and three thousand people watched at least three seconds. Three thousand divided by ten thousand gives a thirty percent hook rate. Track this number for every video. That way you compare openings fairly, using the same measure each time, instead of guessing which one felt stronger.

steps.p: Example: the same 30-second video with four different openings, each with similar spend. The demonstration hook stopped the most people. The numbers are illustrations; your winner will depend on your audience.
steps.say: Now look at the bars. This is an example of the same thirty-second video with four different openings, each with similar spend. The question hook got thirty one percent, the bold statement twenty four, the callout twenty nine, and the demonstration hook led with thirty eight percent. These numbers are illustrations. Your winner will depend on your audience, which is exactly why you test.

steps.p: Example: two videos with the same $3 CPM and 10,000 impressions, so $30 spend each. Video B's stronger hook kept more people watching, more of them clicked, and each click cost much less.
steps.more: Worked example. Video A: 2,000 three-second plays (20% hook rate), 80 link clicks, CTR 0.8%, cost per click $30 ÷ 80 = $0.375. Video B: 3,500 plays (35% hook rate), 140 clicks, CTR 1.4%, cost per click $30 ÷ 140 = $0.214. Same spend, same audience, 43% cheaper clicks. Then check the paid event: a hook that attracts the wrong people can raise CTR and still lose.
steps.say: Why does the hook change your costs? In this example, two videos have the same three dollar C P M, cost per thousand impressions, and ten thousand impressions, so thirty dollars spend each. Video A had a twenty percent hook rate and eighty clicks, so each click cost about thirty seven cents. Video B had a thirty five percent hook rate and a hundred and forty clicks, about twenty one cents each. Same spend, forty three percent cheaper clicks. But still check the paid event, because a hook that attracts the wrong people can raise C T R and still lose.

steps.p: Example: share of viewers still watching at each second for two versions of one ad. Most people leave early. The better hook keeps more viewers at every point after the opening.
steps.say: This curve shows where viewers leave. It's an example of the share still watching at each second, for two versions of one ad. Notice how both lines drop fast at the start, because most people leave early. But the demo-first hook keeps more viewers at every point after the opening than the logo intro. At fifteen seconds, it's twelve percent versus six percent.

steps.p: Most weak openings waste the first seconds on things the viewer does not care about yet. Strong openings show the point straight away, in a way the right person recognises.

b.title: Strong
items: A clear question in big text
A face talking straight to camera
A local setting the viewer knows

steps.say: Compare these two columns. Weak openings waste the first seconds on things the viewer doesn't care about yet: a logo animation, a slow hi guys welcome, tiny text, generic stock footage. Strong openings show the point straight away, in a way the right person recognises: the product on screen at zero seconds, a clear question in big text, a face talking to camera, or a local setting the viewer knows.

steps.p: Most weak hooks fail for the same few reasons. Each one below wastes the most expensive seconds of the ad, the ones you paid an impression for.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Logo or intro in the first second
Judging hooks at very different spend
Text too small for a phone
Choosing the hook by CTR alone
Fake alerts to stop the scroll

steps.say: Most weak hooks fail for the same few reasons. On the left are the mistakes: a logo in the first second, judging hooks at very different spend, text too small for a phone, choosing by C T R alone, and fake alerts to stop the scroll. On the right are the fixes. Show the point at zero seconds, compare at similar spend, use big short text, confirm on the paid event, and use only honest pattern interrupts. Remember, these are the most expensive seconds of your ad.

steps.p: Some hooks get attention by lying: fake breaking news, fake notifications, fake celebrity clips, fake play buttons. They break ad policies, attract the wrong clicks and can get your account restricted. Earn attention honestly.

d.text: No fake news screens, fake system alerts, fake celebrity endorsements or fake profit screenshots.

steps.say: This one matters a lot. Some hooks grab attention by lying: fake breaking news, fake notifications, fake celebrity clips, fake play buttons. They break ad policies, they attract the wrong clicks, and they can get your account restricted. As the warning says, no fake news screens, fake system alerts, fake celebrity endorsements or fake profit screenshots. Earn attention honestly.

steps.p: Once you know which hook types work, you need many openings for the same body. A creative tool can draft variations quickly; a human still checks every claim before upload.

d.why: Draft several hook versions of one ad quickly, then check each one against the hook checklist before testing.

steps.say: Once you know which hook types work, you'll need many openings for the same body. A creative tool like Vooads can draft several hook versions of one ad quickly. But a human still checks every claim before upload, against the hook checklist, before anything goes into a test.

steps.p: Check every new video against this list before you upload. It takes one minute and catches most of the reasons hooks fail or get rejected.
d: Point is clear by second one
Works with sound off, captions on
Text readable on a small phone
steps.say: Finally, here's your hook checklist. Run every new video through it before upload. Is the point clear by second one? Does it work with sound off and captions on? Is the text readable on a small phone? Does it speak to one clear audience? And is there nothing false or misleading? It takes about a minute, and it catches most of the reasons hooks fail or get rejected.

takeaways: The first seconds decide whether the rest of the ad is seen.
Measure hook rate (3-second plays ÷ impressions) and hold rate, then confirm on the paid event.
Earn attention honestly; trick hooks break policy and bring the wrong people.
Hook rate chooses what to iterate; the starting rule card on the paid event decides kill, keep and scale.

lessons.title: Angles and formats
objectives: By the end you can tell an angle from a hook and write several angles for one offer.
You can choose formats such as UGC, talking head, demo and static for each angle.
You can build an angle and format matrix for a test round.
You can read a matrix result and decide which angle earns video budget.

steps.h: Angle is why, hook is how
steps.p: The angle is the reason someone should care: learning, convenience, safety, a problem solved. The hook is how you open the ad. One angle can carry many hooks. Test angles first, because a new angle can find a whole new group of people.
steps.say: Here's the key idea. The angle is why someone should care: learning, convenience, safety, a problem solved. The hook is how you open the ad. One angle can carry many hooks. So test angles first. Why? Because a new angle can find a whole new group of people, while a new hook usually just helps you reach the same people a bit better.

steps.p: These angles fit trading, iGaming and finance offers without promising income. Each one speaks to a different motivation, so each tends to find different people.
d: Product demo|see the app, step by step
Convenience|deposit with M-Pesa or bank app
Safety and control|limits, demo accounts, regulation
Entertainment|the match, the game, for fun
Local relevance|built for your market and language
steps.say: Look at these six angles. They fit trading, iGaming and finance offers without promising income. Education, learn how it works first. Product demo, see the app step by step. Convenience, like depositing with M-Pesa or a bank app. Safety and control, limits, demo accounts, regulation. Entertainment, the match or the game, for fun. And local relevance, built for your market and language. Each speaks to a different motivation, so each tends to find different people.

steps.p: Before writing angles, look at which angles and formats other advertisers in your geo keep running for weeks. Long-running ads are often working. Learn from the angle; never copy the creative.

d.why: See which angles and formats keep running in your geo, so your angle list starts from evidence.

steps.say: Before writing angles, do some research. Look at which angles and formats other advertisers in your geo keep running for weeks. Long-running ads are often working, because few advertisers keep paying for losers. A tool like Spyvoo helps you see this, so your angle list starts from evidence. But remember, learn from the angle, and never copy the creative.

steps.p: Example: angles for a licensed trading app in Ghana. Each line could become several ads with different hooks and formats. None of them promises a result or an income.

rows: What a pip is, in 30 seconds
Watch a trade placed on a demo account
Fund your account with mobile money
Set a stop loss before you trade

steps.say: Here's an example of one offer with five angles, for a licensed trading app in Ghana. Education: what a pip is, in thirty seconds. Demo: watch a trade placed on a demo account. Convenience: fund your account with mobile money. Control: set a stop loss before you trade. Local: support in English and Twi. Each line could become several ads. And notice, none of them promises a result or an income.

steps.p: Format is the shape of the ad. Different formats suit different angles and placements. Build each concept in the format that shows the angle most clearly.
d: UGC|a real person filmed on a phone
Talking head|one presenter speaking to camera
Screen demo|recording of the app or site
Static|one image with a clear message
steps.say: Format is the shape of the ad. Look at the cards. U G C, user-generated content, is a real person filmed on a phone. Talking head is one presenter speaking to camera. Screen demo records the app or site. Static is one image with a clear message. Carousel is several cards, one idea each. And motion graphic uses animated text and visuals. Build each concept in the format that shows the angle most clearly.

steps.p: User-generated content works because it feels like a real person talking. That only stays honest if it is a real person, telling their real experience, with any payment disclosed where required.

a.title: Fake UGC
items: Actor pretends to be a customer

b.title: Honest UGC
items: Real user or clearly a presenter

steps.say: U G C works because it feels like a real person talking. But that only stays honest if it is a real person, telling their real experience, with any payment disclosed where required. Compare the columns. Fake U G C uses actors pretending to be customers, scripted profit claims, undisclosed paid endorsements, or stolen videos. Honest U G C uses a real user or a clear presenter, shows the product not results, discloses paid partnerships, and uses original footage with rights.

steps.h: Every angle must be honest on its own
steps.p: An angle is a reason to care, so it can drift into a promise. 'Convenience' must not become 'easy money'; 'safety' must not become 'no risk'. On regulated offers, each angle still needs the required warnings.

d.text: Disclose paid partnerships where rules require, and never present an actor as a real customer.

steps.say: An angle is a reason to care, so it can slowly drift into a promise. Convenience must not become easy money. Safety must not become no risk. On regulated offers, every angle still needs the required warnings. And as the warning on screen says, disclose paid partnerships where rules require, and never present an actor as a real customer.

steps.p: Most good UGC and talking head scripts follow the same shape. Keep it under about 30 seconds for a first test, and make each part do one job.
steps.say: Here's a simple script shape for U G C and talking head ads. Follow the flow: a hook, then the problem or question, then show the product, then what to expect honestly, then the call to action. Keep it under about thirty seconds for a first test, and make each part do just one job. When a part tries to do two things, it usually does neither well.

steps.p: Example of a short, clear brief sent in a Telegram-style chat. One angle, three hooks to film, what not to say, the format and the disclosure. The creator confirms before filming.

messages.text: Angle: control. Message: you can set a stop loss before you trade. Film 3 hooks: question, demo at 0s, bold true statement.
Not allowed: any income or profit claim, 'no risk', results screenshots. Say 'capital at risk' on camera.
9:16, 20 to 30 s, captions on. Paid partnership disclosed. We keep usage rights for 6 months.
Clear. I will send drafts Thursday.

steps.say: Look at this chat. It's an example of a clear creator brief in a Telegram-style chat. Notice what it covers. One angle, control, with one message. Three hooks to film. A list of what's not allowed: no income or profit claims, no saying no risk, no results screenshots, and say capital at risk on camera. Then the format, nine by sixteen, twenty to thirty seconds, captions on, the disclosure and usage rights. And the creator confirms before filming.

steps.h: Static ads are cheap angle tests
steps.p: A static image with one clear line costs little to make. Use statics to test which angles get clicks and paid events, then spend video budget on the angles that win.

d.text: Test 5 angles as statics, then turn the best 2 into video.

steps.say: Static ads are cheap angle tests. A single image with one clear line costs very little to make. So use statics to find out which angles get clicks and paid events, and then spend your video budget only on the angles that win. As the tip says, test five angles as statics, then turn the best two into video.

steps.h: Build an angle and format matrix
steps.p: Example: three angles crossed with three formats gives nine concepts. Launch them in one test round so you learn which angle wins and which format carries it best.
steps.more: Worked example. 3 angles × 3 formats = 9 concepts. At a $10 target cost per registration and about $30 to read each concept, the round costs about $270. You might find that the demo angle wins in every format, which tells you the angle is strong, or that UGC wins for every angle, which tells you the format is strong. Both are useful.
steps.say: Now let's build a matrix. In this example, three angles, education, convenience and control, cross three formats, U G C, screen demo and static. That gives nine concepts, C zero one to C zero nine. At a ten dollar target and about thirty dollars to read each concept, the round costs about two hundred and seventy dollars. You might learn the angle is strong, if it wins in every format, or the format is strong, if it wins for every angle. Both are useful.

steps.say: These bars show an example of average cost per registration by format across one test round. Here, shorter bars are better. U G C came in at seven dollars eighty, screen demo eight forty, talking head nine ten, and static trailed at eleven twenty. Your results will depend on your geo, offer and audience, so treat this as an illustration, not a rule.

Read across a row to judge the angle, and down a column to judge the format. With a ten dollar target, control wins in every format, from seven sixty with U G C. And static trails in every row. steps.h: Starting rule: which angles get video budget
steps.p: Promote an angle to video only when it has passed the rule card as a static or cheap format: at least 3 conversions and CPA at or under target. Angles that hit a kill rule go to the log, not to production. Adapt to your data.

steps.say: Here's a starting rule for video budget. Promote an angle to video only after it passes the rule card as a static or cheap format: at least three conversions, and C P A, cost per acquisition, at or under target. In this example, target is ten dollars. The control static got four registrations at nine twenty, so it qualifies for video. The convenience static spent thirty dollars for one registration, so it's killed and goes to the log. Adapt this to your data.

steps.p: These mistakes make test rounds expensive and hard to read. Most come from testing small changes before you know which reason to care actually works.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Testing ten hooks on one angle first
Paying for video before angles are proven

b.title: Fixes
items: Learn the angle, make your own

steps.say: These mistakes make test rounds expensive and hard to read. Testing ten hooks on one angle first. Paying for video before angles are proven. Actors posing as customers. Briefs with no banned claims. And copying a competitor's ad. The fixes are on the right: test angles first and hooks second, statics first and video for winners, real users or clear presenters, write the not-allowed list, and learn the angle but make your own.

steps.p: A clear brief saves money and stops creators from improvising claims you cannot use. Give every creator these points in writing before filming starts, and keep a copy with the creative log.
d: The angle and the one message
What the product does and does not do
Words and claims that are not allowed
steps.say: Before you brief a creator, give them these points in writing. The angle and the one message. Three hook options to film. What the product does and does not do. The words and claims that aren't allowed. The format, length and aspect ratios. And the disclosure and usage rights. A clear brief saves money and stops creators improvising claims you can't use. Keep a copy with your creative log.

lessons.title: Creative testing frameworks
objectives: By the end you can set up a creative test with a clear hypothesis and budget.
You can tell a concept test from an iteration test.
You can pick winners on the paid event, not on CTR alone.
You can apply the starting kill and hold rules to each concept in a round.

steps.p: Small changes to a weak idea rarely make it a winner. Big differences between ideas often do. Start by testing different concepts, then iterate on the ones that win. This lesson gives the framework; the Creative testing lab module gives the full step-by-step build.

d.b: Find the idea, then refine it

steps.say: Here's the big idea. Small changes to a weak idea rarely make it a winner. Big differences between ideas often do. So start by testing different concepts, find the idea that works, and only then refine it with iterations. This lesson gives you the framework. The Creative testing lab module gives you the full step-by-step build.

steps.p: These are two different questions. A concept test asks which idea works. An iteration test asks how to make a working idea work better. Mixing them makes results impossible to read.
steps.say: These are two different questions. A concept test asks which idea works. It uses different angles or formats, big differences, it finds new winners, and it fails more often. An iteration test asks how to make a working idea better. Same concept, one change, like the hook, length, creator or C T A, call to action. Smaller but steadier gains. Mix them in one round and the results become impossible to read.

steps.p: Every test should follow the same loop. Writing down the hypothesis before launch stops you from inventing a story after you see the numbers, which is the most common way buyers fool themselves.
steps.say: Every test follows the same loop. Look at the flow: hypothesis, build, launch, read on the paid event, decide, and log the lesson. Writing the hypothesis down before launch is the important part. It stops you inventing a story after you see the numbers, and that's the most common way buyers fool themselves.

steps.p: There is no single correct setup. These are two that operators use. Meta also has a built-in experiments tool for split tests; check the current Ads Manager for its name and options.
steps.more: When many ads share one ad set, Meta often gives most of the spend to one or two ads early. That is efficient for results but unfair as a test. Separate ad sets give each concept a fairer share, at the cost of splitting signal. Many buyers test in a separate campaign, then move winners into their main campaign.

rows: Many ads in one ad set

steps.say: There's no single correct setup, but here are three that operators use. One ad set per concept gives fair spend, but more ad sets. Many ads in one ad set is fast, but Meta often gives most spend to one or two ads early, so spend is uneven. And Meta's built-in split test divides the audience, which is cleanest but needs more budget. Check the current Ads Manager for that tool's name and options. Many buyers test in a separate campaign, then move winners into their main one.

steps.h: Budget a test before you launch
steps.p: Decide how much each concept may spend before you judge it. Example: target cost per registration $10, and you want about three registrations to read a concept. That is $30 each, or $180 for six concepts.
steps.say: Always budget a test before you launch. Decide how much each concept may spend before you judge it. In this example, the target cost per registration is ten dollars, and you want about three registrations to read a concept. That's thirty dollars per concept. Multiply by six concepts, and the round costs one hundred and eighty dollars. Now you know the cost before you spend a cent.

steps.h: The starting kill rules for a test
steps.p: Use the same starting rule card for creatives as for ad sets. Kill at spend ≥ 2 × target with zero results. Once spend reaches 3 × target, kill if CPA is above the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even. Otherwise hold. Adapt for slow events like FTD.
steps.more: Worked example. Target $10 per registration, break-even $14, so the kill line is $14. Concept C04 spends $20 with zero registrations: 2 × target, killed. C05 spends $20 with two registrations, $10 each: hold to the full $30. C06 spends $30 with one registration, a $30 CPA, above $14 after 3 × target: killed and logged. For FTDs, which arrive days later, apply the same rules only to spend whose postbacks have had time to arrive. Full rule card: Budget and kill rules module.

d.text: Example: target $10. $20 spent, 0 results: kill. $30 spent, 1 result ($30 CPA): kill. $20 spent, 2 results: hold.

steps.say: Here are the starting kill rules, the same rule card you use for ad sets. Kill at spend of two times target with zero results. Once spend reaches three times target, kill if the C P A, cost per acquisition, is above the lower of one point five times target and break-even. Otherwise, hold. In the example, target is ten dollars. Twenty spent, zero results: kill. Thirty spent, one result, a thirty dollar C P A: kill. Twenty spent, two results: hold. For slow events like F T D, first-time deposit, give postbacks time to arrive.

steps.p: Apply the starting rule card to one concept from a round. Work out the CPA, check how much it has spent against 3 × target and compare with the kill line. Then press check.
steps.more: Working. CPA $40. Spend is 3.3 × target, so the CPA rule applies. 1.5 × $12 = $18, and $40 is far above it. Kill and log the lesson.

steps.h: The CTR winner is not always the winner
steps.p: Example: three concepts in one test. Creative A had the best CTR and the cheapest registrations, but the worst cost per FTD. B made the most money. Judge on the event you are paid for.
steps.more: Why it happens: a curiosity-heavy hook can attract clickers who are not ready to deposit. A plain demo attracts fewer, more serious people. CTR and hook rate are leading indicators that help you diagnose. Cost per paid event is the result. With small numbers, give FTD data enough time and volume before you decide.

Cost per paid event is the result. And with small numbers, give F T D data enough time and volume before you decide.

steps.p: A generic mock-up of a test sheet at the end of a round. Every concept spent up to 3 × target or hit a kill rule first. The call column is written from the rule card, not from feel.

steps.p: When you iterate on a winner, change one element at a time: the hook, the creator, the length or the CTA. If you change three things and results move, you will not know which change caused it.

d.text: One variable per iteration. Name the ad after the change, for example C05_hookB.

steps.say: When you iterate on a winner, change one element at a time: the hook, the creator, the length or the C T A. If you change three things and results move, you won't know which change caused it. And as the tip says, name the ad after the change, for example C zero five underscore hook B, so your reports explain themselves.

steps.h: Never test whether a false claim passes
steps.p: Some buyers test 'aggressive' versions with income promises or fake urgency to see if they get through review. That breaks ad policy even if the ad runs, and repeated rejections can restrict the account.
steps.more: What repeated rejections can lead to: Ad account bans module.

d.text: Every concept in a test must be one you would happily run at scale.

steps.say: Some buyers test aggressive versions with income promises or fake urgency, just to see if they get through review. Don't do this. It breaks ad policy even if the ad runs, and repeated rejections can restrict the account. The rule on screen is simple: every concept in a test must be one you'd happily run at scale.

steps.p: These mistakes make tests unreadable or expensive. They are easy to avoid if you write the hypothesis, the budget per concept and the rules before launch, and keep to them when a result tempts you.

a.title: Mistakes
items: Mixing concepts and iterations in one round

steps.say: These mistakes make tests unreadable or expensive. Mixing concepts and iterations in one round. No budget per concept. Deciding on C T R. Changing three things at once. And no creative log. The fixes: one question per round, three times target per concept set first, decide on the paid event, one variable per iteration, and log every result and reason. Write the rules before launch, and keep to them when a result tempts you.

steps.h: What to log for every test
steps.p: A creative log turns spend into knowledge your whole team can reuse. Over months it becomes the most valuable document in your operation, because it records what worked, what failed and why.
d: Creative ID, angle, format and hook

The decision and the reason. And the lesson for the next round. lessons.title: Fatigue and iteration
objectives: By the end you can spot creative fatigue from frequency, CTR and cost trends.
You can calculate how a falling CTR raises your cost per FTD.
You can plan an iteration ladder and a weekly creative calendar.
You can apply starting fatigue rules next to your rule card.

steps.p: The same people see your ad again and again. At first that helps. Then they stop noticing it, CTR falls and costs rise. This is creative fatigue, and planning for it is part of the job.

d.s: Plan the next one before you need it

steps.say: Here's something every buyer learns. The same people see your ad again and again. At first that helps. Then they stop noticing it, C T R, click-through rate, falls, and costs rise. That's creative fatigue. As the screen says, winners have a shelf life. So plan the next one before you need it. That planning is part of the job.

steps.p: Frequency is the average number of times each person saw your ad. Example: 42,000 impressions reached 12,000 people, so the frequency is 3.5. Watch it by ad set over a set period, such as seven days.
steps.say: Frequency is the average number of times each person saw your ad. In this example, forty two thousand impressions reached twelve thousand people. Forty two thousand divided by twelve thousand gives a frequency of three point five. Watch frequency by ad set over a set period, such as seven days, so you're comparing like with like.

steps.p: No single number proves fatigue. Look for several of these moving together over a week, on an ad that used to perform. If only one moves, look for another cause first.
steps.say: No single number proves fatigue. Look at the table. Frequency rising. C T R and hook rate falling. C P M, cost per thousand impressions, often rising. Cost per paid event rising. And comments getting more negative or repetitive. Look for several of these moving together over a week, on an ad that used to perform. If only one moves, look for another cause first.

steps.h: Spotting fatigue in a weekly breakdown
steps.p: A generic mock-up of one winning ad broken down by week. Several signals move together: frequency up, CTR down, cost per FTD up. That pattern, not one bad day, is fatigue.
steps.more: Worked example. Best CTR 1.6%, now 1.0%: a fall of 0.6 points, which is 37.5% of 1.6. Cost per FTD rose from $20 to $31. With a $30 target and $40 break-even, the ad is still above target but under the kill line, so the rule card says Hold, and the fatigue rule says brief new iterations.

blocks.value: CTR down about 38% from its best, frequency rising. Brief iterations now.

steps.say: Here's a mock-up of one winning ad broken down by week. Notice how the signals move together. Frequency goes from one point six to three point eight. C T R falls from one point six percent to one percent, about thirty eight percent off its best. Cost per F T D, first-time deposit, rises from twenty to thirty one dollars. With a thirty dollar target and forty dollar break-even, the rule card says hold, and the fatigue rule says brief new iterations now.

steps.h: How a falling CTR raises cost
steps.p: Example: CPM stays at $4 and 1.25% of clicks become FTDs. When CTR drops from 1.6% to 1.0%, cost per FTD rises from $20 to $32. Nothing else changed.
steps.more: Worked example. Cost per FTD = CPM ÷ (1,000 × CTR × click-to-FTD rate). At 1.6% CTR: $4 ÷ (1,000 × 0.016 × 0.0125) = $4 ÷ 0.2 = $20. At 1.0% CTR: $4 ÷ (1,000 × 0.010 × 0.0125) = $4 ÷ 0.125 = $32. A CTR drop that looks small on screen is a 60% rise in cost per FTD.

d.label: cost per FTD after CTR fell to 1.0%

steps.say: Let's see how a falling C T R raises cost. In this example, C P M stays at four dollars, and one point two five percent of clicks become F T Ds. When C T R drops from one point six percent to one percent, cost per F T D rises from twenty dollars to thirty two, the number on screen. Nothing else changed. A C T R drop that looks small is a sixty percent rise in cost per F T D.

steps.p: Example: weekly cost per FTD for two ad sets that started with the same winning ad. One kept running it alone. The other added a new iteration every week. The refreshed ad set stayed near target.
steps.say: Look at these two lines. It's an example of weekly cost per F T D for two ad sets that started with the same winning ad. One kept running that ad alone, and its cost climbed from twenty dollars to thirty four by week seven. The other added a new iteration every week, and it stayed near twenty to twenty one dollars, close to target. Refreshing keeps a winner alive.

steps.p: These rules sit next to your rule card. They do not replace it: kills still come from the card. They decide when to stop adding budget and when to brief new creative. Starting rules; adapt to your data.
steps.more: These match the stop-scaling rules in the Budget and kill rules module. The 30% line is a starting habit, not a platform number; tune it to how fast your ads tire.

rows: CTR down 30%+ from its best, frequency rising
No more budget steps; brief 2 to 3 iterations
CPA since last step above 0.8 × target for 48 h
CPA above the kill line after 3 × target
New iteration passes the rule card
Let it carry volume, then pause the old ad

steps.say: These fatigue rules sit next to your rule card; kills still come from the card. If C T R is down thirty percent or more from its best and frequency is rising, take no more budget steps and brief two to three iterations. If C P A, cost per acquisition, since the last step is above point eight times target for forty eight hours, no more steps, just keep. If C P A is above the kill line after three times target, kill it. And when a new iteration passes, let it carry volume, then pause the old ad. The thirty percent line is a starting habit. Adapt to your data.

steps.p: Start with the cheapest change that could restore attention and keep the core that made the ad win. Move down the ladder only when the cheaper steps stop working.
steps.say: Here's the iteration ladder. Start with the cheapest change that could restore attention, and keep the core that made the ad win. A new hook first. Then a new first frame. Then a new creator or voice. Then a new length or pace. And finally a new format, same angle. Move down the ladder only when the cheaper steps stop working.

steps.h: What to keep, what to change
steps.p: A winner wins for a reason, usually its angle and its core message. Keep those. Change the surface so the same people see something that feels new.
steps.say: A winner wins for a reason, usually its angle and core message. So look at the cards. Keep the angle and core message. Keep the offer and the honest claims. Change the opening seconds. Change the face, voice or setting. You're changing the surface, so the same people see something that feels new, while the reason it works stays the same.

steps.p: When a winner starts to tire, add new iterations next to it rather than pausing it at once. Let delivery move to the new ads as they prove themselves. Pausing a winner too early can leave you with nothing working.

d.text: Add 2 to 3 new iterations to the ad set. Pause the old winner only once a new one carries the volume.

steps.say: When a winner starts to tire, don't pause it straight away. Add new iterations next to it, and let delivery move to the new ads as they prove themselves. Pausing too early can leave you with nothing working. As the tip says, add two to three new iterations to the ad set, and pause the old winner only once a new one carries the volume.

steps.h: Every iteration goes through review again
steps.p: A new hook is a new ad. It must keep the honest claims and any required risk or age warning, even when the edit is quick. Never re-upload a rejected ad with small changes to slip past review.
steps.more: What repeated rejections can lead to: Ad account bans module.

d.text: Iterate the surface, never the honesty: claims, warnings and disclosures stay.

steps.say: Remember, a new hook is a new ad, and it goes through review again. It must keep the honest claims and any required risk or age warning, even when the edit is quick. And never re-upload a rejected ad with small changes to slip past review. As the warning says, iterate the surface, never the honesty. Claims, warnings and disclosures stay.

steps.p: Fatigue costs most when buyers react late or react to the wrong signal. These are the usual errors, and the fix for each one, so you react early and to the right signal.

items: Pausing the winner before a new ad works
Calling fatigue on one bad day
Changing the angle when only the hook tired
Raising budget to fight falling CTR

b.title: Fixes
items: Look for several signals over a week
Climb the iteration ladder in order
Stop budget steps when CTR falls 30%+
Brief every week, even when winning

steps.say: Fatigue costs most when buyers react late, or react to the wrong signal. The mistakes: pausing the winner before a new ad works, calling fatigue on one bad day, changing the angle when only the hook tired, raising budget to fight falling C T R, and having no iterations briefed in advance. The fixes: add iterations then pause, look for several signals over a week, climb the ladder in order, stop budget steps when C T R falls thirty percent or more, and brief every week.

steps.p: Dchessking on why his media buying team at Zedapex plans and briefs new creative every week, even when the current ads are still performing well across their geos.
steps.d: The best time to make your next winner is while the current one is still working. Once it dies, you are already late.

steps.p: A steady rhythm beats panic production. This is an example cadence for a small team; adjust it to your budget and how fast your ads tire.
d: Monday: review last week's creative log
Tuesday: brief 2 to 3 iterations of winners
Friday: launch in planned test slots

Adjust it to your budget and how fast your ads tire.

takeaways: Fatigue shows as rising frequency and cost with falling CTR and hook rate, together over time.
Small CTR drops cause large cost rises: cost per FTD = CPM ÷ (1,000 × CTR × CR).
Iterate the surface, keep the angle, add new ads before pausing winners, and keep a weekly rhythm.
When CTR falls 30%+ from its best with frequency rising, stop budget steps and brief iterations; kills still come from the rule card.

lessons.title: Localisation, honest copy and AI tools
objectives: By the end you can localise an ad for language, money, payment methods and setting.
You can write copy that is persuasive and honest, and reply to sceptical comments.
You can use AI tools to speed up creative work without faking people, results or claims.
You can run an AI-drafted script through a pre-check and native speaker review before launch.

steps.p: A translated ad says the same words in another language. A localised ad feels like it was made in that place: the right language, money, payment methods, faces, places and timing. People respond to ads that feel like theirs.
steps.say: A translated ad says the same words in another language. A localised ad feels like it was made in that place. It has the right language, money, payment methods, faces, places and timing. As the screen says, it feels local, not translated. People respond to ads that feel like theirs, so this is worth the extra effort.

steps.p: Most of these markets use more than one language. Testing a local language version next to English often finds new audiences. Have a native speaker check every script.
d: South Africa|English, Zulu, Afrikaans and more
steps.say: Look at the cards. Most of our core markets use more than one language. Nigeria has English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa and Igbo. Kenya has English, Swahili and Sheng. Ghana has English, Twi and others. Cameroon has French and English, plus Pidgin. South Africa has English, Zulu, Afrikaans and more. Testing a local language version next to English often finds new audiences. And always have a native speaker check every script.

steps.p: Language is only one part. Check each of these for every geo you run, and change them in the creative, the copy and the landing page so the whole journey matches.
d: Payment methods, such as M-Pesa or mobile money
Faces, settings and places people know
steps.say: Language is only one part. Check each of these for every geo. Currency and realistic amounts. Payment methods, such as M-Pesa or mobile money. Faces, settings and places people know. Time zone and posting hours. Local events, holidays and fixtures. And local rules and required warnings. Change them in the creative, the copy and the landing page, so the whole journey matches.

steps.p: Honest copy can still be strong. It is specific about what the product does, clear about risk, and gives one simple next step. It avoids promises nobody can keep.

b.title: Honest and strong
items: Practise free on a demo account first
Licensed by the regulator named on site

steps.say: Honest copy can still be strong. Compare the columns. Misleading copy says earn fifty k daily guaranteed, zero risk, only three spots left when that's untrue, or bank-approved when it isn't. Honest and strong copy says practise free on a demo account first, capital at risk, start small, sign-up takes about three minutes, licensed by the regulator named on site. It's specific about what the product does, clear about risk, and gives one simple next step.

steps.p: Comments are part of your creative. Honest, calm replies build trust with everyone reading them. Never promise income in a reply, even when someone asks for it directly.

d.text: Is this real? Can I make 50k a day with this app?
Nobody can promise daily income. It is a trading app and your money is at risk. Try the free demo account first and see if it is for you.

steps.say: Comments are part of your creative. In this chat, a lead asks if they can make fifty k a day. Notice the reply: nobody can promise daily income, it's a trading app and your money is at risk, try the free demo first. Then they ask about funding with Opay, and the buyer points them to the deposit page to check the options. Calm, honest replies build trust with everyone reading. Never promise income in a reply, even when someone asks directly.

steps.p: AI tools can make a small team much faster. Use them to speed up the work around a real, honest message, with a human checking everything before it goes live.
d: Script drafts|many hooks from one brief
Translation drafts|checked by a native speaker
Compliance pre-checks|flag risky claims before review
steps.say: A I tools can make a small team much faster. Look at the good uses. Script drafts, many hooks from one brief. Translation drafts, checked by a native speaker. Voiceovers, with licensed voices and honest scripts. Resizing and edits, into nine by sixteen, four by five and one by one. And compliance pre-checks, flagging risky claims before review. The rule is simple: A I speeds up the work around a real, honest message, and a human checks everything before it goes live.

steps.p: The same tools can produce fakes that mislead people and break platform rules. If a viewer would believe something false about who is speaking or what happened, do not publish it.

a.title: Never
items: AI people presented as real customers
Deepfakes of celebrities or real people

steps.say: The same tools can produce fakes. No budget step; keep the budget and brief 2 to 3 iterations first
Double the budget before fatigue gets worse
exam.why: The fatigue rule comes first: CTR down 30%+ from its best with rising frequency means no more steps until new creatives carry volume, even when CPA qualifies.
